```{r}
#| label: pipeline
# Shared setup for every section: load, clean, split, recipe, prep
library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse, tidymodels, here, gt, GGally)
tidymodels_prefer()

# load data
phones <- here("data/smartphone_cleaned_v5.csv") |>
read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# 1. Data Cleaning
# - remove the 2 luxury editions where their price comes from gold/materials
# - perform transformation, log the price as it is heavily right-skewed
# - recode 5G and NFC to Yes/No so the dummy names are readable
# - keeps the 7 biggest brands, pool the rest into "Other", and make "xiaomi" the base reference level.
# - keeps only the 12 variables used, then drop incomplete rows.
pca_vars <- c("processor_speed", "ram_capacity", "internal_memory",
              "refresh_rate", "primary_camera_rear", "primary_camera_front")

phones_clean <- phones |>
  filter(!model %in% c("Vertu Signature Touch", 
                       "Xiaomi Redmi K20 Pro Signature Edition")) |>
  mutate(
    log_price = log(price),
    has_5g = factor(if_else(as.logical(has_5g), "Yes", "No"), 
                    levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    has_nfc = factor(if_else(as.logical(has_nfc), "Yes", "No"),
                     levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    brand_group = fct_relevel(fct_lump_n(brand_name, n = 7), "xiaomi")
  ) |>
  select(log_price, all_of(pca_vars), battery_capacity, screen_size, has_5g,
         has_nfc, brand_group) |>
  na.omit()
```

```{r}
# 2. Split: 75% training, 25% testing
set.seed(41352)
phone_split <- initial_split(phones_clean, prop = 0.75, strata = log_price)
phone_training <- training(phone_split)
phone_test <- testing(phone_split)
```

```{r}
# 3. Recipe: normalise -> PCA on the 6 specifications -> dummy variables -> drop constants
phone_rec <- recipe(log_price ~ ., data = phone_training) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_pca(all_of(pca_vars), threshold = 0.7, id = "pca") |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())
```

```{r}
# 4. Prep
phone_prep <- prep(phone_rec)
```

# Introduction {background-color="#1f4e79" style="text-align: center;"}

## Dataset and business question {.smaller}

::: notes
**Step 6: Prepare A's labels and sample counts**

The following chunks stay in the combined document. They read the shared data and create only A's own objects. Count luxury removals separately from records removed for missing values. a_labels makes the tables easier to read.
:::

```{r a-counts-labels, include=FALSE}
a_eligible <- phones |>
  filter(!model %in% c("Vertu Signature Touch",
                       "Xiaomi Redmi K20 Pro Signature Edition"))
a_luxury_removed <- nrow(phones) - nrow(a_eligible)
a_incomplete_removed <- nrow(a_eligible) - nrow(phones_clean)
a_labels <- c(
  price = "Price (₹)",
  log_price = "Log price",
  processor_speed = "Processor speed (GHz)",
  ram_capacity = "RAM (GB)",
  internal_memory = "Storage (GB)",
  refresh_rate = "Refresh rate (Hz)",
  primary_camera_rear = "Rear camera (MP)",
  primary_camera_front = "Front camera (MP)",
  battery_capacity = "Battery capacity (mAh)",
  screen_size = "Screen size (inches)",
  has_5g = "5G", has_nfc = "NFC", brand_name = "Brand"
)
```

::: notes
**Step 7: Calculate the correlation used in the justification**

Use the six PCA variables and the same complete records as B. Keep pca_vars as a character vector of names, rather than replacing it with a data frame. B's section provides the correlation plot.
:::

```{r a-correlation, include=FALSE}
a_pca_data <- phones_clean |>
  select(all_of(pca_vars))
a_cor <- cor(a_pca_data)
```

::: notes
**Step 8: Prepare descriptive summaries**

Calculate the mean, standard deviation, median, minimum and maximum for each numeric analysis variable. pivot_longer() gives one row per variable. The summaries describe all complete records before splitting, while PCA is fitted on the training sample.
:::

```{r a-numeric-summaries, include=FALSE}
a_numeric_summary <- phones_clean |>
  summarise(across(
    where(is.numeric),
    list(mean = mean, sd = sd, median = median, min = min, max = max),
    .names = "{.col}__{.fn}"
  )) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", ".value"), names_sep = "__")
```

::: notes
**Step 9: Count missing values in the used source variables**

Count missing values after removing the two luxury editions and before dropping incomplete rows. Use price and brand_name here because they generate log_price and brand_group. Missing fields can occur in the same record, so their counts do not equal the number of removed phones.
:::

```{r a-missing-counts, include=FALSE}
a_source_vars <- c("price", pca_vars, "battery_capacity", "screen_size",
                   "has_5g", "has_nfc", "brand_name")
a_missing <- a_eligible |>
  summarise(across(all_of(a_source_vars), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing")
```

::: {style="margin-top: 60px;"}
**What drives smartphone prices in the Indian market: overall specifications, specification trade-offs or brand?**

- **`r nrow(phones)` smartphone models/variants**, `r ncol(phones)` original variables.
- **Indian market**, with prices retained in **Indian rupees (₹)**.
- **Business context:** pricing and competitive positioning.
- **Kaggle dataset**, with the full citation on the References slide near the end.
:::

::: notes
One record is a listed smartphone model or variant, not a buyer. These are observational data, so "drives" means statistical associations in this presentation. Market context and ₹ follow the group's stated context. The original source's currency definition has not been independently verified. Prices describe the dataset snapshot, not current market prices. ## Outcome and extra predictors {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 30px; margin-bottom: 30px;"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-a-other-vars
#| tbl-cap: "Outcome and extra predictors (not used in the PCA)"
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
tibble(
  variable = c("price", "log_price", "battery_capacity", "screen_size",
               "has_5g", "has_nfc", "brand_group"),
  type = c("Numeric", "Numeric", "Numeric", "Numeric",
           "Categorical", "Categorical", "Categorical"),
  role = c("Listed price (₹), used to create the outcome",
           "Natural log of price in ₹, the outcome",
           "Battery capacity (mAh)", "Screen diagonal (inches)",
           "5G available, No / Yes", "NFC available, No / Yes",
           "Top seven brands plus Other, Xiaomi reference")
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(variable = "Variable", type = "Type", role = "Meaning / role") |>
  opt_table_outline() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(18),
              column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
              column_labels.vlines.style = "solid",
              table_body.vlines.style = "solid")
```
:::

- **Five extra predictors:** two numeric and three categorical (@tbl-a-other-vars).
- Price and these extra predictors are **excluded from PCA construction**.

::: notes
The five extra predictors are battery capacity, screen size, 5G, NFC and brand group. B standardises battery and screen size for regression, but they do not enter step_pca(). NFC means near-field communication. log_price is the natural log of the numerical ₹ price, not itself a rupee amount. No currency conversion is performed.

Two source variables are used in preparation only. model is a text identifier used to remove the two specified luxury editions. brand_name is the original categorical manufacturer used to create brand_group. The named brands are Apple, Motorola, Oppo, Realme, Samsung, Vivo and Xiaomi. Other pools the remaining manufacturers. Xiaomi, no 5G and no NFC are the reference categories for D's regression. Each retained PC is a weighted combination of the six standardised specifications.
:::

## Why this dataset suits PCA {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 30px;"}
- **Business relevance:** compare specification bundles and product positioning.
- **Shared information:** RAM and storage correlate at **`r round(a_cor["ram_capacity", "internal_memory"], 2)`** in the complete records.
- **Suitable structure:** six numeric PCA inputs, a numeric outcome, and numeric and categorical extra predictors.
- **Usable sample:** **`r nrow(phones_clean)` complete records**, with **`r nrow(phone_training)`** used to fit PCA.
:::

::: notes
The correlation is computed on exactly the same complete records as B's correlation plot. A strong correlation indicates shared information, not a causal effect. B's section shows the detailed correlation evidence and explains how many components are kept.
:::

## Why use log price? {.smaller}

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-a-price
#| fig-cap: "Price and natural log of price for the retained phones"
#| fig-height: 3.5
phones_clean |>
  transmute(price = exp(log_price), log_price) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measure = factor(measure, levels = c("price", "log_price"),
                          labels = c("Price (₹)", "Log price"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#1f4e79", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free", ncol = 2, strip.position = "bottom") +
  scale_x_continuous(n.breaks = 4, labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of phones") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 15))
```
:::

- **`r nrow(phones_clean)` retained phones**, matching the analysis sample (@fig-a-price).
- Log price **compresses the upper tail** and supports interpreting proportional price differences.

::: notes
exp(log_price) recovers the original numerical ₹ prices for the same complete records without changing phones_clean. The two panels have different horizontal scales. A skewed outcome alone does not violate linear regression assumptions. Taking logs is a modelling choice, not proof that assumptions are satisfied. Scenario 6 requires fitting and interpreting the model, not evaluating predictive performance.
:::

# Data preparation and PCA {background-color="#1F4E79" style="text-align: center;"}

```{r}
#| label: corr-numbers
# Numbers used in the text of this slide
nice_names <- c(
  processor_speed = "Processor speed",
  ram_capacity = "RAM",
  internal_memory = "Internal memory",
  refresh_rate = "Refresh rate",
  primary_camera_rear = "Rear camera",
  primary_camera_front = "Front camera"
)

pca_data <- phones_clean |>
  select(all_of(pca_vars))

# Full correlation table for heatmap
cor_full <- cor(pca_data) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("v1") |>
  pivot_longer(-v1, names_to = "v2", values_to = "r") |>
  mutate(v1 = unname(nice_names[v1]),
         v2 = unname(nice_names[v2]))

# One copy of each pair (v1 < v2) for the strongest and weakest pair
cor_long <- cor_full |>
  filter(v1 < v2)

top_pair <- slice_max(cor_long, r, n = 1)
low_pair <- slice_min(cor_long, r, n = 1)
mean_r <- mean(cor_long$r)
```

## Are the specifications correlated? {.smaller}

:::::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-corr
#| fig-cap: "Correlations among the six specifications used in the PCA."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
pca_data |>
  rename_with(~ unname(nice_names[.x])) |>
  ggpairs(upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 6)),
          lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", size = 0.4, alpha = 0.3))) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```
:::

:::::: {.column width="42%"}
::: incremental
- **Correlations** range from `r round(low_pair$r, 2)` to `r round(top_pair$r, 2)`, with an average of `r round(mean_r, 2)`.

- **Strongest pair:** `r top_pair$v1` and `r top_pair$v2` (`r round(top_pair$r, 2)`); **weakest:** `r low_pair$v1` and `r low_pair$v2` (`r round(low_pair$r, 2)`).

- The specifications **overlap**, so **PCA** can combine them into **fewer** uncorrelated components.
:::

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-tip title="So what"}
Phones can be compared on a few overall specification levels instead of six separate numbers.
:::
::::
::::::
::::::::

::: notes
The scatter plot matrix is the evidence that PCA suits the data. If the variables were unrelated, PCA would not be able to summarise them.
:::

## Method and justification {.smaller}

::: {style="margin-top: 40px;"}
```{r}
#| label: method-table
tibble(
  choice = c("<strong>PCA</strong> on six specifications",
             "<strong>Standardise</strong> before PCA",
             "<strong>Linear regression</strong>",
             "<strong>Variables left out</strong>"),
  reason = c("Specifications overlap (<span data-qmd=\"@fig-corr\">Figure 2</span>); a few uncorrelated components avoid multicollinearity.",
             "Units differ (GB, GHz, Hz, MP); stops large numbers from dominating.",
             "Log price is numeric; the question is what drives price.",
             "Rating: largely explained by the specifications. Fast charging: missing for most iPhones.")
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_passthrough(columns = c(choice, reason), escape = FALSE) |>
  cols_label(choice = "Choice", reason = "Reason") |>
  opt_table_outline() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(18),
              column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
              column_labels.vlines.style = "solid",
              table_body.vlines.style = "solid")
```
:::

::: notes
Normalise comes before the dummy step so that the 0/1 dummy variables are not rescaled.
:::

## Preprocessing steps {.smaller}

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
1.  **Standardise** all numeric predictors.
    - Fair weighting in PCA.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
2.  **Combine** the six specifications into **principal components** that explain at least 70% of the variance.
    - Removes overlap and keeps key information.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
3.  Turn 5G, NFC and brand into 0/1 **dummy variables.**
    - Regression requires numbers; done after standardising so they stay 0/1.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
4.  **Drop** any **column** with a **single value**.
    - Avoids useless predictors.
:::

## Variance explained {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: var-numbers
var_tbl <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "variance")

# number of components kept = number of PC columns after bake()
n_pc <- bake(phone_prep, new_data = NULL) |>
  select(starts_with("PC")) |>
  ncol()

pc1_var <- var_tbl |>
  filter(terms == "percent variance", component == 1) |>
  pull(value)

cum_var <- var_tbl |>
  filter(terms == "cumulative percent variance", component == n_pc) |>
  pull(value)

# variance of the first component that is not kept
next_var <- var_tbl |>
  filter(terms == "percent variance", component == n_pc + 1) |>
  pull(value)

var_wide <- var_tbl |>
  filter(terms %in% c("percent variance", "cumulative percent variance")) |>
  select(component, terms, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = terms, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(component = paste0("PC", component))
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-var
#| tbl-cap: "Variance explained by each principal component."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
var_wide |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(component = "Component",
             `percent variance` = "Variance (%)",
             `cumulative percent variance` = "Cumulative (%)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(`percent variance`, `cumulative percent variance`),
             decimals = 1) |>
  opt_table_outline() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(18),
              column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
              column_labels.vlines.style = "solid",
              table_body.vlines.style = "solid")
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-scree
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of variance explained by each component."
#| fig-width: 6

ggplot(var_wide, aes(component, `percent variance`)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C7FB8") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(`percent variance`, 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = "Component", y = "Percentage of variance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```
:::
:::::

::: notes
Percent variance is the share of the total information that each component holds. PC1 always holds the most.
:::

## Number of components retained {.smaller}

::: incremental
- **PC1** explains **`r round(pc1_var, 1)`%** of the variance in the six specifications (@tbl-var, @fig-scree).

- The first **`r n_pc` PCs** together explain **`r round(cum_var, 1)`%**, meeting the **70% threshold**.

- Each remaining component adds only **`r round(next_var, 1)`% or less**.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip title="So what"}
**`r n_pc` PCs are kept:** each phone is described by `r n_pc` components instead of six specifications, with little loss of information.
:::

::: notes
The 70% threshold is set in step_pca(). R keeps the smallest number of components whose cumulative variance reaches 70%.
:::

```{r}
#| label: c-objects
#| output: false
# Person C objects. Uses phone_prep and phone_training from Person B.

# 1. Loadings: one row per specification x component (Week 7/8 PCA lecture)
pca_loadings <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "coef")

# Number of components kept by threshold = 0.7 (= PC columns after bake)
c_pc_scores <- bake(phone_prep, new_data = NULL) |>
  select(starts_with("PC"))
kept_pcs <- names(c_pc_scores)

# Variance explained by the kept components (for the text)
c_var <- tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "variance")
pc_pct <- c_var |>
  filter(terms == "percent variance", component <= length(kept_pcs)) |>
  pull(value)
pc_cum <- c_var |>
  filter(terms == "cumulative percent variance",
         component == length(kept_pcs)) |>
  pull(value)

# Readable names for the six specifications (units in brackets)
spec_vars <- c("processor_speed", "ram_capacity", "internal_memory",
               "refresh_rate", "primary_camera_rear", "primary_camera_front")
spec_labels <- c(
  processor_speed      = "Processor speed (GHz)",
  ram_capacity         = "RAM (GB)",
  internal_memory      = "Storage (GB)",
  refresh_rate         = "Refresh rate (Hz)",
  primary_camera_rear  = "Rear camera (MP)",
  primary_camera_front = "Front camera (MP)"
)

# Group style for charts: same colours and fonts as styles.css
theme_slides <- function(base_size = 16) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(text = element_text(colour = "#1F2933"),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = "#5F6B7A"),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#E6ECF2"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1F4E79",
                                    size = rel(1.05), hjust = 0),
          legend.position = "top",
          legend.justification = "left")
}

# Group style for gt tables: same style as the other tables in the deck
slide_table <- function(tbl, font_px = 18) {
  tbl |>
    opt_table_outline() |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = px(font_px),
                column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
                column_labels.vlines.style = "solid",
                table_body.vlines.style = "solid")
}

# Loading of one specification on one component (used in the text)
ld <- function(pc, spec) {
  pca_loadings |>
    filter(component == pc, terms == spec) |>
    pull(value) |>
    round(2)
}

# Sign check: signs can flip between computers (Week 7/8 lecture).
# Both must be TRUE for the component names below to be correct.
pc1_loadings <- pca_loadings |>
  filter(component == "PC1") |>
  pull(value)
pc1_all_positive <- all(pc1_loadings > 0)
pc2_storage_vs_camera <- ld("PC2", "internal_memory") > 0 &
  ld("PC2", "primary_camera_rear") < 0

# 2. Part (a) descriptive analysis: average specifications of phones with
#    low, middle and high component scores. bake() replaces the six specs
#    with PC1 and PC2, so join the scores back to the original training rows.
pc_profile <- bind_cols(phone_training, c_pc_scores)

profile_long <- map_dfr(kept_pcs, \(pc) {
  pc_profile |>
    mutate(group = ntile(.data[[pc]], 3),
           group = factor(group, levels = 1:3,
                          labels = c("Low", "Middle", "High"))) |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarise(phones = n(), across(all_of(spec_vars), mean),
              price = median(exp(log_price))) |>
    pivot_longer(-group, names_to = "spec", values_to = "mean") |>
    mutate(component = pc)
})

# Average of one specification in one group (used in the text)
avg <- function(pc, grp, spec, digits = 0) {
  profile_long |>
    filter(component == pc, group == grp, spec == !!spec) |>
    pull(mean) |>
    round(digits)
}

# 3. Price map data: the training phones with their names, prices and
#    which side of PC2 they fall on. Rows of phone_training are
#    phones_clean[phone_split$in_id, ], so the model names line up exactly.
phones_named <- phones |>
  filter(!model %in% c("Vertu Signature Touch",
                       "Xiaomi Redmi K20 Pro Signature Edition")) |>
  select(model, price, all_of(spec_vars), battery_capacity, screen_size,
         has_5g, has_nfc, brand_name) |>
  na.omit()
# Safety check: same phones in the same order as phones_clean
stopifnot(nrow(phones_named) == nrow(phones_clean),
          all(phones_named[spec_vars] == phones_clean[spec_vars]))

# Prices are kept in the dataset's original currency, Indian rupees (₹).

phone_map <- pc_profile |>
  mutate(model = phones_named$model[phone_split$in_id],
         price = exp(log_price),
         focus = if_else(PC2 > 0, "Memory and speed focused", "Camera focused"),
         focus = factor(focus, levels = c("Memory and speed focused",
                                          "Camera focused")))

# Five well-known phones to label, with label offsets so they do not overlap
example_phones <- tribble(
  ~model,                        ~label,             ~nudge_x, ~nudge_y,
  "Redmi 12C",                   "Redmi 12C",         0.3,     -0.45,
  "Nothing Phone 1",             "Nothing Phone 1",   0.0,     -0.55,
  "OnePlus 11 5G",               "OnePlus 11",       -0.2,      0.40,
  "Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra 5G", "Galaxy S23 Ultra",  0.2,      0.38,
  "Apple iPhone 13",             "iPhone 13",        -0.9,      0.30
) |>
  inner_join(phone_map |> select(model, PC1, price, focus), by = "model")

focus_colours <- c("Memory and speed focused" = "#2C7FB8",
                   "Camera focused" = "#D95F02")

# Correlation between PC1 and log price (used in the text)
pc1_price_cor <- round(cor(phone_map$PC1, phone_map$log_price), 2)

# Price in rupees of one labelled phone (used in the text)
ex_price <- function(phone) {
  example_phones |>
    filter(label == phone) |>
    pull(price) |>
    round() |>
    scales::comma()
}

# One "low vs high" row for the part (a) slide: label | low | high
stat_row <- function(pc, spec, label, unit, digits = 0, down = FALSE) {
  show <- function(x) {
    if (unit == "₹") scales::comma(x) else paste(x, unit)
  }
  lo <- show(avg(pc, "Low", spec, digits))
  hi <- show(avg(pc, "High", spec, digits))
  cls <- if (down) "stat down" else "stat"
  paste0('<div class="', cls, '"><span class="stat-label">', label,
         '</span><span class="stat-low">', lo,
         '</span><span class="stat-value">', hi, "</span></div>")
}

# Wide table for a slide: rows = specifications, columns = Low / Middle / High
profile_table <- function(pc) {
  profile_long |>
    filter(component == pc) |>
    select(-component) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = mean) |>
    mutate(spec = case_when(spec == "phones" ~ "Phones",
                            spec == "price" ~ "Median price (₹)",
                            .default = unname(spec_labels[spec]))) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(spec = "Specification (average)") |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Low, Middle, High), decimals = 1) |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Low, Middle, High),
               rows = spec == "Processor speed (GHz)", decimals = 2) |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Low, Middle, High),
               rows = spec %in% c("Phones", "Median price (₹)"),
               decimals = 0) |>
    slide_table(font_px = 17)
}

# Median price of one third, formatted (used in the text)
third_price <- function(pc, grp) {
  avg(pc, grp, "price") |> scales::comma()
}

# 4. Share of each specification kept by the retained components
#    (communality = sum over kept PCs of loading^2 x eigenvalue)
pc_eigen <- c_var |>
  filter(terms == "variance", component <= length(kept_pcs)) |>
  arrange(component) |>
  pull(value)
share_kept <- pca_loadings |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  mutate(eigen = pc_eigen[parse_number(component)]) |>
  group_by(terms) |>
  summarise(kept = 100 * sum(value^2 * eigen))
kept_pct <- function(spec) {
  share_kept |> filter(terms == spec) |> pull(kept) |> round()
}
# Specification name without its unit, e.g. "Refresh rate"
spec_name <- function(spec) str_remove(unname(spec_labels[spec]), " \\(.*\\)")
kept_min <- share_kept |> slice_min(kept, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
kept_max <- share_kept |> slice_max(kept, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
# All specifications that round to the lowest share (e.g. two at 62%)
kept_low_names <- share_kept |>
  filter(round(kept) == round(kept_min$kept)) |>
  pull(terms) |>
  spec_name() |>
  str_to_lower() |>
  str_flatten(collapse = ", ", last = " and ")

# 5. Market positioning map: phones split by the sign of their PC1 score
#    (budget vs flagship side) and PC2 score (camera vs memory focus)
quadrants <- phone_map |>
  mutate(tier = factor(if_else(PC1 > 0, "Flagship side", "Budget side"),
                       levels = c("Budget side", "Flagship side"))) |>
  group_by(tier, focus) |>
  summarise(phones = n(),
            median_price = median(price),
            nfc = 100 * mean(has_nfc == "Yes"),
            .groups = "drop")

# Median price and NFC share of one cell, formatted (used in the text)
q_price <- function(tier, focus) {
  quadrants |>
    filter(tier == !!tier, str_starts(as.character(focus), !!focus)) |>
    pull(median_price) |> round() |> scales::comma()
}
q_nfc <- function(tier, focus) {
  quadrants |>
    filter(tier == !!tier, str_starts(as.character(focus), !!focus)) |>
    pull(nfc) |> round()
}

# Trend-line price for each colour group at a typical budget score (10th
# percentile of PC1) and a typical flagship score (90th percentile).
# Same straight-line fit on log price as the lines in the price map.
pc1_budget <- quantile(phone_map$PC1, 0.10)
pc1_flagship <- quantile(phone_map$PC1, 0.90)
trend_price <- function(focus, score) {
  group <- filter(phone_map, str_starts(as.character(focus), !!focus))
  fit <- lm(log(price) ~ PC1, data = group)
  exp(predict(fit, tibble(PC1 = score))) |> round(-2) |> scales::comma()
}

# iPhone 13 against phones with a similar overall performance score
iphone_pc1 <- example_phones |> filter(label == "iPhone 13") |> pull(PC1)
similar_price <- phone_map |>
  filter(abs(PC1 - iphone_pc1) < 0.25, brand_group != "apple") |>
  summarise(n = n(), median = median(price))
```

# What do the components mean? {background-color="#1f4e79" style="text-align: center;"}

## How each specification loads {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-loadings
#| tbl-cap: "Loadings on each retained component and the share of each specification they keep."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
pca_loadings |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = terms, names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  left_join(share_kept, by = "terms") |>
  mutate(terms = unname(spec_labels[terms])) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(terms = "Specification", kept = "Kept (%)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = all_of(kept_pcs), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = kept, decimals = 0) |>
  slide_table(font_px = 22)
```
:::

::::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.card .navy}
[How to read the table]{.kicker}

**Loading:** from −1 to 1, how strongly a specification moves with a component. Further from 0 = stronger link.

**Kept:** share of a specification's variation that PC1 and PC2 hold together.
:::

::: fragment
- **PC1:** every loading is **positive** (@tbl-loadings)
- **PC2:** storage and processor speed **positive**, both cameras **negative**, refresh rate close to **0** (@tbl-loadings)
- **Kept:** from `r round(kept_min$kept)`% (`r kept_low_names`) to `r round(kept_max$kept)`% (`r spec_name(kept_max$terms)`) (@tbl-loadings)
:::
:::::
:::::::

::: notes
The loadings come from B's prepped recipe with tidy(phone_prep, id = "pca", type = "coef"); "pca" is the id B gave to step_pca. Only the components kept by the 70% threshold are shown. "Kept" is the communality: for each specification, the sum over PC1 and PC2 of the squared loading times the component's eigenvalue (variance). It tells us how well two components represent each original specification. The weakest are refresh rate and the front camera (about `r round(kept_min$kept)`%), so the remaining variation in those two sits in the components that were dropped. If asked about the code, open the .qmd: the c-objects chunk computes these values.
:::

## Two components describe the hardware {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-top-loadings
#| fig-cap: "The three largest loadings on each component. Blue = positive, orange = negative."
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 5.4
pca_loadings |>
  filter(component %in% kept_pcs) |>
  group_by(component) |>
  slice_max(abs(value), n = 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(spec = fct_reorder(unname(spec_labels[terms]), abs(value)),
         sign = if_else(value > 0, "Positive", "Negative")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = abs(value), y = spec, fill = sign)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ component, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Positive = "#2C7FB8", Negative = "#D95F02")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.8), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Absolute loading", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_slides()
```
:::

::::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .fragment}
[PC1 · `r round(pc_pct[1], 1)`% of the variance]{.kicker} [Overall performance]{.big}

- All six loadings are **positive** (`r round(min(pc1_loadings), 2)` to `r round(max(pc1_loadings), 2)`), led by RAM (@tbl-loadings)
- Phones strong in one specification tend to be strong in the others (@fig-top-loadings)
:::

::: {.card .orange .fragment}
[PC2 · `r round(pc_pct[2], 1)`% of the variance]{.kicker} [Storage and speed vs camera]{.big}

- Storage (`r ld("PC2", "internal_memory")`) and processor speed (`r ld("PC2", "processor_speed")`) **positive**; rear (`r ld("PC2", "primary_camera_rear")`) and front cameras (`r ld("PC2", "primary_camera_front")`) **negative** (@tbl-loadings)
- Refresh rate is close to 0 (`r ld("PC2", "refresh_rate")`), so PC2 does not reflect it (@tbl-loadings)
- A **balance**, not a level: phones lean towards memory or towards cameras (@fig-top-loadings)
:::
:::::
:::::::

::: notes
@tbl-loadings shows all loadings and @fig-top-loadings shows the three largest per component. Same colour means the specifications move together; opposite colours mean a trade-off. Before rotation, all variables tend to load highly on the first component, as the PCA lecture explains, which is why PC1 is an overall factor. PC2 is a contrast: a high score means storage and speed are high relative to the cameras, not that a phone has a lot of storage in absolute terms. Sign check for this render: PC1 all positive = `r pc1_all_positive`; PC2 storage positive and rear camera negative = `r pc2_storage_vs_camera`. If either is FALSE, the signs flipped on this computer: swap "high" and "low" in the wording on this slide and the following ones.
:::

## What high and low PC1 scores look like {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-pc1-profile
#| tbl-cap: "Averages by PC1 third (training phones)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
profile_table("PC1")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| output: asis
cat('<div class="stat-head"><span>Low vs high PC1</span><span>Low</span><span>High</span></div>',
    stat_row("PC1", "ram_capacity", "RAM", "GB", digits = 1),
    stat_row("PC1", "internal_memory", "Storage", "GB"),
    stat_row("PC1", "refresh_rate", "Refresh rate", "Hz"),
    stat_row("PC1", "primary_camera_rear", "Rear camera", "MP"),
    stat_row("PC1", "price", "Median price (₹)", "₹"),
    sep = "\n")
```

[**Every** specification and the median price rise from low to high: PC1 separates **budget** from **flagship** phones (@tbl-pc1-profile).]{.note-line}
:::
:::::

::: notes
This is the descriptive analysis the brief asks for in part (a): the components are described with the six variables that built them. The `r nrow(pc_profile)` training phones are split into three equal groups by score with ntile(), and the original specifications are averaged in each group (@tbl-pc1-profile, @tbl-pc2-profile). The last row is the median price, because price is right-skewed and a few flagships would pull a mean upwards. The right-hand rows repeat the clearest low and high values from the table. Blue = higher for high scorers; orange = lower for high scorers. These are descriptive averages, not significance tests.
:::

## What high and low PC2 scores look like {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-pc2-profile
#| tbl-cap: "Averages by PC2 third (training phones)."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
profile_table("PC2")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| output: asis
cat('<div class="stat-head"><span>Low vs high PC2</span><span>Low</span><span>High</span></div>',
    stat_row("PC2", "internal_memory", "Storage", "GB"),
    stat_row("PC2", "ram_capacity", "RAM", "GB", digits = 1),
    stat_row("PC2", "primary_camera_rear", "Rear camera", "MP", down = TRUE),
    stat_row("PC2", "primary_camera_front", "Front camera", "MP", down = TRUE),
    stat_row("PC2", "price", "Median price (₹)", "₹"),
    sep = "\n")
```

[A **balance**: high scorers carry more storage, low scorers bigger cameras. The middle third has the least storage (`r avg("PC2", "Middle", "internal_memory")` GB) (@tbl-pc2-profile).]{.note-line}
:::
:::::

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-tip title="Why it matters"}
Two levers position a phone: **how much hardware** it has (PC1) and **where that hardware goes** (PC2).
:::
::::

::: notes
PC2 is a balance, which is why the middle third has the least storage (`r avg("PC2", "Middle", "internal_memory")` GB) and the lowest median price (₹`r third_price("PC2", "Middle")`): those phones are average on both memory and cameras. These are descriptive averages, not significance tests.
:::

## Better-equipped phones cost more {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-price-map
#| fig-cap: "Price (₹) against overall performance score. Blue = leans towards memory and speed (PC2 above 0); orange = leans towards cameras (PC2 below 0). Lines show each group's trend."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.6
phone_map |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = price, colour = focus)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = example_phones, size = 3.5, shape = 21,
             fill = "white", stroke = 1.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_label(data = example_phones,
             aes(x = PC1 + nudge_x, y = price * exp(nudge_y), label = label),
             colour = "#1F2933", fill = "white", size = 4.2,
             label.size = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(),
                breaks = c(5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000, 200000)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = focus_colours) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 3))) +
  labs(x = "Overall performance score (PC1): low = budget, high = flagship",
       y = "Price in rupees (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_slides()
```
:::

::::: {.column width="40%"}
::: fragment
[`r pc1_price_cor`]{.hero} [correlation between PC1 and log price]{.kicker}

[Redmi 12C ₹`r ex_price("Redmi 12C")` to Galaxy S23 Ultra ₹`r ex_price("Galaxy S23 Ultra")` (@fig-price-map)]{.note-line}
:::

::: fragment
- **Lines split at the top:** typical flagship ₹`r trend_price("Memory", pc1_flagship)` (memory) vs ₹`r trend_price("Camera", pc1_flagship)` (camera); typical budget phone ₹`r trend_price("Memory", pc1_budget)` vs ₹`r trend_price("Camera", pc1_budget)` (@fig-price-map)
- **iPhone 13:** ₹`r ex_price("iPhone 13")`, against ₹`r scales::comma(round(similar_price$median))` for phones with a similar PC1 score (@fig-price-map)
:::
:::::
:::::::

::: notes
Each dot is one training phone. The x-axis is the PC1 score. Colour splits phones by the sign of their PC2 score: blue = above 0 (memory and speed), orange = below 0 (camera). Each line is a straight-line trend of log price on PC1 within one group. "Typical flagship" = the 90th percentile of PC1 (score `r round(pc1_flagship, 1)`), "typical budget phone" = the 10th percentile (score `r round(pc1_budget, 1)`); the prices are read off the two trend lines (budget: ₹`r trend_price("Memory", pc1_budget)` memory-focused vs ₹`r trend_price("Camera", pc1_budget)` camera-focused). The gap between the lines grows with performance, so the extra paid for memory is largest among flagships; the next slide shows this directly. A similar PC1 score for the iPhone 13 = the `r similar_price$n` non-Apple phones whose PC1 score is within 0.25 of the iPhone 13's. Price is on a log scale because it is right-skewed; equal steps up the axis are equal percentage increases. Prices are in Indian rupees (₹), the currency recorded in the dataset. These are descriptive patterns; the regression controls for the other predictors.
:::

## The memory premium is largest among flagships {.smaller}

:::::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-positioning
#| fig-cap: "Median price (₹) of the training phones in each corner of the PC1 × PC2 map (split at 0 on each score)."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.8
quadrants |>
  mutate(focus = fct_recode(fct_rev(focus),
                            "Camera focused\n(PC2 below 0)" = "Camera focused",
                            "Memory and speed\nfocused (PC2 above 0)" = "Memory and speed focused"),
         tier = fct_recode(tier,
                           "Budget side\n(PC1 below 0)" = "Budget side",
                           "Flagship side\n(PC1 above 0)" = "Flagship side"),
         ink = if_else(median_price > 30000, "white", "#1F2933")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = focus, y = tier, fill = median_price)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(round(median_price)),
                colour = ink), fontface = "bold", size = 7.5, vjust = -0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(phones, " phones\n", round(nfc), "% with NFC"),
                colour = ink), size = 4.6, vjust = 1.2, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#DCEAF6", high = "#1F4E79", guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  labs(x = "Where the hardware goes (PC2)", y = "How much hardware (PC1)") +
  theme_slides() +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 13, colour = "#1F2933"))
```
:::

:::::: {.column width="45%"}
::: fragment
- **Flagships:** memory ₹`r q_price("Flagship side", "Memory")` vs camera ₹`r q_price("Flagship side", "Camera")` (@fig-positioning)
- **Budget phones:** no clear premium; camera ₹`r q_price("Budget side", "Camera")` vs memory ₹`r q_price("Budget side", "Memory")` (@fig-positioning)
- **NFC:** `r q_nfc("Flagship side", "Memory")`% of memory-focused flagships vs `r q_nfc("Flagship side", "Camera")`% of camera-focused ones (@fig-positioning)
:::

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-tip title="So what"}
Storage and speed go with the highest prices **at the top end**; budget phones can lead on cameras at a similar price.
:::
::::
::::::
::::::::

::: notes
Each training phone is placed in one of four corners by the sign of its two scores: PC1 above or below 0 (flagship or budget side) and PC2 above or below 0 (memory or camera focus). Each tile shows the median price, the number of phones and the share with NFC. The regression finds a positive PC2 effect (@tbl-specs); that is an average over all phones. This map shows where it comes from: the gap is large among flagships and small among budget phones. Memory-focused budget phones are also weaker overall (lower PC1), so the two budget tiles are not a like-for-like comparison; at the same PC1, the trend lines on the previous slide put memory-focused phones slightly higher. Part of the flagship gap travels with connectivity, since memory-focused flagships have NFC more often; the regression separates these effects. Medians are descriptive, so no significance claim is made here.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fit-model
#| output: false

linear_model <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

phone_wkfl <- workflow() |>
  add_model(linear_model) |>
  add_recipe(phone_rec)

phone_fit <- phone_wkfl |>
  fit(data = phone_training)

phone_results <- phone_fit |>
  extract_fit_parsnip() |>
  tidy() |>
  mutate(significance = case_when(p.value < 0.001 ~ "0.1%",
                                  p.value < 0.01 ~ "1%",
                                  p.value < 0.05 ~ "5%",
                                  TRUE ~ "Not significant"),
         # readable names for the slides
         label = case_when(term == "(Intercept)" ~ "Intercept",
                           term == "battery_capacity" ~ "Battery capacity",
                           term == "screen_size" ~ "Screen size",
                           term == "PC1" ~ "PC1: overall performance",
                           term == "PC2" ~ "PC2: storage and speed vs camera",
                           term == "has_5g_Yes" ~ "5G (vs no 5G)",
                           term == "has_nfc_Yes" ~ "NFC (vs no NFC)",
                           term == "brand_group_apple" ~ "Apple",
                           term == "brand_group_motorola" ~ "Motorola",
                           term == "brand_group_oppo" ~ "Oppo",
                           term == "brand_group_realme" ~ "Realme",
                           term == "brand_group_samsung" ~ "Samsung",
                           term == "brand_group_vivo" ~ "Vivo",
                           term == "brand_group_Other" ~ "Other brands"))

# the 7 brand dummies (each compared with Xiaomi, the base category)
brand_terms <- c("brand_group_apple", "brand_group_motorola", "brand_group_oppo",
                 "brand_group_realme", "brand_group_samsung", "brand_group_vivo",
                 "brand_group_Other")
```

```{r}
#| label: base-levels
#| output: false
# base category = first level of each factor
levels(phones_clean$has_5g)
levels(phones_clean$has_nfc)
levels(phones_clean$brand_group)
```

# Regression Results {background-color="#1f4e79" style="text-align: center;"}

## What drives smartphone prices? {.smaller}

Dependent variable: **log price**. Base categories: **Xiaomi**, **no 5G**, **no NFC**. We read the **significance level** and the **sign** only, not the size of each coefficient.

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-specs
#| tbl-cap: "Components, specifications and features"
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
phone_results |>
  filter(!term %in% brand_terms) |>
  select(label, estimate, p.value, significance) |>
  mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 3),
         p.value = case_when(p.value < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
                             TRUE ~ format(round(p.value, 4), nsmall = 4))) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(label = "Term", estimate = "Coefficient",
             p.value = "p-value", significance = "Significance") |>
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(p.value, significance)) |>
  opt_table_outline() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(18),
              column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
              column_labels.vlines.style = "solid",
              table_body.vlines.style = "solid")
```
:::

::: {.column width="3%"}
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-brands
#| tbl-cap: "Brands compared with Xiaomi"
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
phone_results |>
  filter(term %in% brand_terms) |>
  select(label, estimate, p.value, significance) |>
  mutate(estimate = round(estimate, 3),
         p.value = case_when(p.value < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
                             TRUE ~ format(round(p.value, 4), nsmall = 4))) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(label = "Brand", estimate = "Coefficient",
             p.value = "p-value", significance = "Significance") |>
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(p.value, significance)) |>
  opt_table_outline() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(18),
              column_labels.font.weight = "bold",
              column_labels.vlines.style = "solid",
              table_body.vlines.style = "solid")
```
:::
::::::

::: notes
Linear regression fitted on the training data with the tidymodels workflow. As the brief asks, we only fit and interpret the model; we do not evaluate its fit or prediction. A positive sign means a higher log price, and so a higher price.
:::

## Specifications vs price {.smaller}

::: incremental
- **Overall performance (PC1):** **positive significant influence** on price at the **0.1% level** (@tbl-specs); stronger all-round phones are priced higher.
- **Storage and speed vs camera (PC2):** **positive significant influence** at the **0.1% level**; storage- and speed-focused phones are priced higher than camera-focused ones.
- **Screen size:** **positive significant influence** at the **0.1% level**; larger screens, higher price.
- **Battery capacity:** **negative significant influence** at the **0.1% level**; larger batteries, lower price.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip title="So what"}
Price rises with the overall performance bundle and screen size; bigger batteries are linked to lower prices, and extra camera megapixels alone do not raise price.
:::

::: notes
All four effects hold after taking the other variables in the model into account. PC1 and PC2 are named from their loadings on the previous slides. PC1: processor, RAM, storage, refresh rate and both cameras all load positively, so a higher PC1 means a stronger all-round phone. PC2: storage and processor load positively and the two cameras negatively, so among phones with similar overall performance, a higher PC2 means a storage- and speed-focused phone. Large batteries are a main selling point of budget phones, which likely explains the negative sign.
:::

## Features and brands vs price {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: brand-data
#| output: false
brand_results <- phone_results |>
  filter(term %in% brand_terms)
```

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-brand
#| fig-cap: "Brand coefficients compared with Xiaomi (blue = significant at 5%, grey = not significant)"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
brand_results |>
  ggplot(aes(label, estimate, fill = p.value < 0.05)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2C7FB8", "FALSE" = "#9AA5B1")) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Brand", y = "Coefficient (log price) vs Xiaomi") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)
```
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment
- Phones **with NFC:** significantly **higher** price than without NFC (0.1% level).
- Phones **with 5G:** significantly **higher** price than without 5G (5% level).
- **Apple, Samsung** (0.1%) and **Vivo** (1%): significantly **higher** than Xiaomi (@tbl-brands, @fig-brand).
- **Motorola:** significantly **lower** than Xiaomi (1% level).
- **Oppo, Realme** and **other brands:** **not significantly different** from Xiaomi.
:::
::::
::::::

::: notes
Every brand comparison is against Xiaomi, the base category, for phones with similar specifications and features. So the brand gap is a brand premium, not a difference in hardware.
:::

# Summary {background-color="#1f4e79" style="text-align: center;"}

## Key findings {.smaller}

::::::: {.grid2 .compact}
::: {.card .navy .fragment}
[1 · PCA]{.kicker} [Two components summarise the hardware]{.big}

Overall performance (PC1) and storage and speed vs camera (PC2) explain `r round(pc_cum, 1)`% of the variation in the six specifications (@tbl-loadings, @fig-top-loadings)

[**Use:** compare a phone with its rivals on 2 scores instead of 6 specifications]{.so}
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[2 · Specifications]{.kicker} [Better-equipped phones cost more]{.big}

Both components and screen size raise price at the 0.1% level; a larger battery lowers it (@tbl-specs)

[**Size:** median ₹`r third_price("PC1", "Low")` (low PC1 third) vs ₹`r third_price("PC1", "High")` (high third) (@tbl-pc1-profile)]{.so}
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
[3 · Connectivity]{.kicker} [NFC and 5G add a premium]{.big}

NFC at the 0.1% level and 5G at the 5% level, compared with phones without them (@tbl-specs)

[**Where:** NFC in `r q_nfc("Flagship side", "Memory")`% of memory-focused flagships vs `r q_nfc("Budget side", "Camera")`% of camera-focused budget phones (@fig-positioning)]{.so}
:::

::: {.card .orange .fragment}
[4 · Brand]{.kicker} [Brand matters beyond hardware]{.big}

Apple, Samsung and Vivo are priced above Xiaomi, Motorola below; Oppo, Realme and Other do not differ (@tbl-brands)

[**Example:** iPhone 13 at ₹`r ex_price("iPhone 13")` vs ₹`r scales::comma(round(similar_price$median))` for phones with a similar PC1 score (@fig-price-map)]{.so}
:::
:::::::

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-important title="Bottom line"}
Price follows the **whole hardware bundle** and the **brand name**. The memory premium is largest among flagships (₹`r q_price("Flagship side", "Memory")` vs ₹`r q_price("Flagship side", "Camera")`), with no clear gap among budget phones (@fig-positioning, @tbl-specs).
:::
::::

::: notes
Card 1 comes from the PCA (B and C). Cards 2 to 4 come from the regression (D) and were checked against the seed 41352 output: PC1, PC2, screen size, battery, NFC, Apple and Samsung at 0.1%; Vivo and Motorola at 1%; 5G at 5%; Oppo, Realme and Other not significant. "Raise price" means a positive significant influence on log price, holding the other variables constant. The lines starting with Use, Size, Where and Example are descriptive figures from the training phones (medians and shares), not regression coefficients. The bottom line combines D's positive PC2 result with the positioning map: the PC2 effect is an average, and the descriptive gap is concentrated among flagships.
:::

# Recommendations {background-color="#1f4e79" style="text-align: center;"}

## Recommendation 1: performance

::: {.callout-note title="Finding"}
Overall performance (PC1) and the storage and speed focus (PC2) both have a **positive significant influence** on price at the 0.1% level, while battery capacity has a **negative** one (@tbl-specs).
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip title="Action for manufacturers"}
- To launch a **higher-priced model**, upgrade the **whole performance bundle**: processor, RAM, storage, refresh rate and cameras together.
- At the **same overall performance**, favour **storage and processing** over extra camera megapixels: storage- and speed-focused phones are priced higher than camera-focused ones, most of all among flagships (@fig-positioning).
- Use **large batteries** to add value to **budget models**, not to charge more.
:::

::: notes
This recommendation turns the two PCA components into a product design rule for manufacturers.
:::

## Recommendation 2: brand gap

::: {.callout-note title="Finding"}
With similar specifications, **Apple, Samsung and Vivo** are priced significantly **higher** than Xiaomi, while **Oppo and Realme** are not significantly different and **Motorola** is **lower** (@tbl-brands, @fig-brand).
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip title="Action for retailers and brands"}
- Display **Xiaomi** phones next to **Samsung and Vivo** models with matching specifications, and promote them as **"same specifications, lower price"**.
- **Motorola**, priced below Xiaomi, should compete on **specifications per price** rather than raise prices.
:::

::: notes
This recommendation uses the brand effects, which hold after controlling for specifications, so the gap is brand value rather than better hardware. Only Xiaomi is named in the display action because every brand coefficient is measured against Xiaomi.
:::
